paras: The threatened lynching of Tom Hawkins took place in Mono County, California, in November 1880, when citizens of Bridgeport formed a Vigilance Committee to hang Hawkins, a gambler accused of shooting Henry Robbins on election day. Officials moved Hawkins to Bodie and then, after threats there, to Aurora, Nevada, and no report says he was harmed. The story ran in Nevada and California dailies as a short item in Bodie wire dispatches, and none of them stated the race of either man.

According to a dispatch from Bridgeport to the Bodie Free Press, a man was shot in the breast and dangerously wounded by "a gambler named Tom Hawkins" about 6 p.m. on November 2, 1880. That dispatch named the wounded man as Roberts and gave "a political difference" as the supposed cause, while later Bodie dispatches called him Henry Robbins and placed the shooting at Bridgeport on election day. Even on the first evening there was talk of lynching Hawkins if Robbins died.

By November 8 the citizens of Bridgeport and vicinity had formed themselves into a Vigilance Committee to hang Hawkins. The prisoner was taken to Bodie for safe keeping, but citizens there also threatened to lynch him, and he was removed across the state line to Aurora. The Bodie correspondent called the shooting "cold-blooded" and predicted that Hawkins "will not escape hanging if he is brought back to the county jail."

A further dispatch of November 9 reported "some talk" of a Vigilance Committee for both Hawkins and Job Draper, a man arrested at Bodie for killing his wife, adding that it "may or may not result in anything."
No report on whether Robbins lived or died, whether Hawkins was returned to Mono County, or any trial appears in the coverage.

The Eureka Daily Sentinel printed the first account on November 7, crediting a Bridgeport dispatch to the Bodie Free Press. The Bodie dispatch of November 8 then ran in the Gold Hill Daily News, the Sacramento Daily Record-Union and the Eureka Sentinel, with the name printed as T. E. Hawkins or, in Gold Hill, "T. E. Hamkins." The Record-Union set the item under the heading "Wife Murder—Judge Lynch Abroad" and summarized it in its news digest, where the shooting was placed "at Bodie."

The papers repeated the correspondent's verdict that the shooting was cold-blooded and did not question the committee. On November 12 the Eureka Sentinel's local column noted that a Vigilance Committee was talked of at Bodie and remarked that "there are other places that need them badly." No paper described Hawkins or Robbins by race.

A Vigilance Committee of Bridgeport citizens intended to hang Hawkins for shooting Robbins, but he was removed to Aurora and no paper reports that he was killed (A3, A4); this was a threatened lynching only.
A Nov. 2 Bridgeport dispatch to the Bodie Free Press (A2) and separate Bodie dispatches of Nov. 8 and Nov. 9 (A3, A4, A7, A8) agree that Hawkins shot Robbins and was threatened with lynching.
